summary: The two claims the split rests on check out against the tree: SubscriptionHub.publishSegment gathers targets across every run and calls streamTo once (SubscriptionHub.java:343-387, 499-502, the only production streamTo call site), AssembledServingPathTest.aSegmentOfMANYRunsIsReadONCENotOncePerRun builds an 8-run delta and asserts gets()-getsBefore == 1 so a per-run loop reds it at 8, the ~178-of-~1,600 figure derives from docs/research/00-problem/02-cost-model.md:136, SegmentProxy.java's javadoc does carry the per-consumer rule, each Push does carry its own run's key/recordCount/firstOffset, the Tracking failure-path description is accurate, and SPEC R11 (M5/SPEC.md:299) plus M5.16 do own the cache. The division into a and b is sound. One major defect: M5.40a's Serves cell cites NFR-4 (read request rate) for a defect the row itself says leaves the request count at 1, and never names NFR-5, the requirement it actually breaks by ~5 orders of magnitude.

findings.title: M5.40a cites NFR-4 for a byte defect its own text says costs no requests, and never names NFR-5
findings.failure_scenario: The row's Serves cell is NFR-4, whose target in requirements.md:33 is 'Read request rate | scales with segments, AZs, nodes -- never with shards, partitions or indices'. The row's own body says 'THE GET COUNT STAYS 1', so by its own account the read request rate is untouched and NFR-4 is not at risk. What the duplication does break is NFR-5 (requirements.md:34, 'Cross-AZ bytes < 0.1% of ingested bytes'), which the row never mentions. The magnitude is not a rounding error: one Target per (subscription, run) means total push bytes for one segment are (runs in segment) x (segment size) = 1,600 x 8 MiB = 12.8 GiB per 8 MiB segment, ~1,600x the ingested bytes, with roughly two thirds of it crossing an AZ boundary to consumers in the other two AZs. Against a 0.1% budget that is about five orders of magnitude over. Consequence for whoever picks the row up: it reads as tidiness ('this is pod BANDWIDTH ... the waste is real') under a requirement that is already satisfied, so it is priced as low and its acceptance criterion will be written against a GET count that is already 1 and always was. Fix is one cell and one clause: Serves NFR-5 (add NFR-4 only with a sentence saying why a byte defect is cited against a request-rate requirement), and state the amplification as a number so the row carries its own severity. M5.40b's NFR-4 is fine by contrast -- cost.md rule 5 'One fetch per object per node' is the operationalisation of NFR-4's 'scales with ... nodes', and exceeding it is a request-rate defect.

findings.title: M5.40b sends the taker to a measurement that cannot see the ceiling it demands
findings.failure_scenario: The cell closes with 'a cache is a new residency bound, so it owes an eviction rule and a memory ceiling that criterion 6's flat-in-K measurement can see'. M5/SPEC.md:342 defines criterion 6 as 'serving an N MiB segment to K consumers holds service memory flat in K, at K = 1 and K = 64, with a bound independent of K', and M5.12's row records that it is asserted as an EQUALITY between K=1 and K=64. A cache of capacity C adds the same C at both K, so the equality holds and the criterion passes identically whether C is 8 MiB or 8 GiB. A taker who follows this sentence implements a cache, sees criterion 6 stay green, and ships an unbounded residency with the row's own evidence behind it. The cache ceiling needs its own assertion (residency at rest, independent of K), not criterion 6.

findings.title: 'names this row as carrying it' is one hop off: the javadoc names M5.40, not M5.40a
findings.failure_scenario: SegmentProxy.java's per-consumer paragraph ends '...no test can see it, because every test in this file measures a single call; M5.40 carries it.' M5.40a says the javadoc 'names this row as carrying it'. After this commit M5.40's State cell redirects, so a reader still arrives -- but the same one-hop staleness is what this very commit found in M5.39 and M5.12, and the diff does not update the javadoc that is now one row out of date. Not worth a fix round on its own; worth doing in the commit that takes M5.40a, which touches that javadoc anyway.

notes: Split judgement: sound, and not deferral. The two remainders have disjoint mechanisms and disjoint fixes -- M5.40a is duplicate sinks within ONE publish (a cache cannot help: the bytes are already read once and handed over K times), M5.40b is repeat reads across SEPARATE publishes (a call-site rule cannot help: the second publish does not exist when the first is served). They also have disjoint surfaces: M5.40a is a Subscriber/Push contract change reaching six test bridges plus a failure-semantics decision (all-K-fail or none), M5.40b is a new component with an eviction rule and a memory ceiling behind or beside the BinStore seam. Either one alone is a full commit; together they would be the shape review.md rule 12 exists to prevent. In-flight coalescing is correctly left inside M5.40b rather than treated as a third path: a joiner arriving mid-read can only be served a suffix unless the bytes are retained, and retaining them is the cache.

Scope: the diff is one row rewritten and two added, all inside the current-milestone table. No scope widening. The closure claim on M5.40's first half is genuinely load-bearing on committed code (d944a24 M5.45a), not on the working tree.

Neither new row names M5.43, which will wire `direct` and will face the identical (node, segment)-versus-run granularity question on the grant side that M5.40a faces on the sink side -- M5.39's closing cell states the rule for it. Not a finding; a cross-reference worth one clause when M5.40a is taken.
Cosmetic: M5.40b writes 'Doc 10 s4' where every other occurrence in the file writes 'Doc 10 s4' as 'Doc 10 SECTION 4' with the section sign. Not worth a round.
